title: Commentary on the Gospel of John
subtitle: Selections from the twelve books
source: Summarized from the Library of Fathers translation by P. E. Pusey (1874-1885), public domain. Marginal notes by the editors of Purify.

sections.title: The eternal Word
paragraphs: Cyril opens his commentary at the only place a commentary on John can begin: the eternal generation of the Son from the Father. Against the Arians of his day, who still survived in Egypt, he insists that 'In the beginning' means before all beginnings, before the world, before time, before any thought of creation. The Word was not made the Son; the Word always was the Son.

Cyril's reading is governed by a single rule: whatever is said of the Word must be said of one Person, the same who is begotten of the Father eternally and who is born of the Virgin in time. This Person is the subject of every verse of the Gospel. The Word who was with God in chapter one is the same Word who weeps at the tomb of Lazarus, who is crucified, who rises. To divide the verses between two subjects, as the Nestorians later would, is to read another Gospel.
notes: Cyril wrote this commentary before the Nestorian controversy erupted, but the rule it establishes, one Person, one subject, two natures undivided, became the rule the Council of Ephesus made the Church's own.
P. E. Pusey's nineteenth-century English translation, the basis for these selections, is reissued by Orthodox publishers under various titles and remains the most accessible English Cyril.

sections.title: The Paraclete
paragraphs: In his ninth book Cyril reaches the discourses of John 14-16, where Christ promises the coming of the Spirit. Cyril reads the promise within the doctrine of the Trinity that the Gospel has been building from its opening verse. The Spirit who comes is not other than God; He proceeds from the Father and is given by the Son, and His coming is the way the Father and the Son make their home with the believer.

Cyril is careful with the phrase 'whom the Father will send in my name'. The Spirit comes in the name of the Son because He has the same nature as the Son and the Father; what the Spirit teaches will not contradict what the Son has already spoken. The Christian who is taught by the Spirit is being conformed to Christ, not led elsewhere.
notes: Cyril's reading of the Paraclete is the foundation of the later Orthodox refusal to add 'and the Son' (filioque) to the Creed of 381. Procession and mission are distinct categories: the Spirit proceeds from the Father, and is sent by the Son in time.
These two short selections are the entry points; Cyril's full commentary, twelve books long, is one of the largest works of patristic exegesis ever written.
